newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives portray Blair as German puppet.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives portray Blair as German puppet.

text.p: The ruling Conservatives on Friday put aside their own deep splits over Europe to portray opposition leader Tony Blair as a German puppet who would sit back and allow Bonn to dictate the pace of European integration.

In their most brutal pre-election assault on the Labour party chief so far, the Conservatives ran several full-page advertisments picturing Blair as a tiny ventriloquist's dummy sitting on the knee of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

"Don't send a boy to do a man's job. You can only be sure with the Conservatives," read the slogan, hammering home the message that Prime Minister John Major was the best man to defend Britain's interests in Europe.
But with less than two weeks to go before a May 1 election, Major himself is still battling to stop his party from tearing itself apart over the contentious issue of a European Union single currency.

On Thursday he offered a key concession to the vocal band of Conservative rebels opposed to the idea, saying he would not be against the idea of allowing members of parliament a free vote on whether or not to join a single currency which is planned for 1999.

Major, frustrated by the amount of time spent on the issues of Europe and sleaze, hoped the new offer would quieten the malcontents in his camp and focus their ire on Labour, which still enjoys a commanding opinion poll lead.
But Major's comments on a free vote surprised the government -- including pro-European finance minister Kenneth Clarke -- and prompted attacks by Blair and usually pro-Conservative papers.
"There are two Tory parties and John Major is in charge of neither of them. They are unravelling in chaos and disarray," Blair told reporters in Edinburgh.
"The divergence between between John Major and his party is marked and growing," said the right-wing Times broadsheet.

"The attempt to finesse that dissent with the hastily floated prospect of a free vote has only confused, not defused matters," it said, predicting the next Conservative leader would be reject any further integration with the European Union.

Major refuses to rule out membership of a single European currency -- which a large chunk of his party fears would mean sacrificing the country's sovereignty -- and government policy is to wait and see if it is in Britain's interest to join.
But much to his anger, two junior ministers and more than 200 Conservative candidates have vowed to campaign against the country joining a single currency under any circumstances.
The Daily Express newspaper on Friday said a junior Home Office (interior) minister, David Maclean, had joined the rebels by issuing an election pamphlet describing a single currency as disastrous.
"What a hopeless shambles the Tories have become," the tabloid Sun said. The paper, which has traditionally backed the Conservatives, has already declared it is supporting Blair.

"How will a man whose own party ignore him be able to get Europe to sit up and take notice? Major's got more chance of making it rain," the paper said in a reference to the drought afflicting some parts of England.
Major was also given short shrift by a live television audience late on Thursday, which laughed and jeered at him several times when he tried to defend his record.
But, despite his troubles, he will draw some consolation from a poll for Friday's Independent newspaper which showed Labour's lead had slipped by three percentage points in the past week.
